vignette:
**Patient Name:** Amara K. (pseudonym)
**Age:** 37
**Occupation:** Co-owner of a small ethnic grocery and spice shop
**Trauma:** Sexual assault by a trusted community member (roughly 14 months prior)

Amara comes to session with a rigid posture, sitting at the edge of the chair, her purse clutched in her lap like a shield. She speaks in a low, careful voice, often glancing toward the door. She is a shopowner, a role she once loved. For ten years, she and her husband, Raj, ran "The Spice Route," a small grocery store in a quiet strip mall. It was her sanctuary—the smell of cumin and cardamom, the regular customers who called her by name, the satisfaction of stacking cans of ghee and bags of basmati rice in neat rows.

The assault happened fourteen months ago, after a community Diwali celebration. A man she had known for years—a respected elder in the temple committee—offered to help her carry boxes of leftover decorations to her car. She trusted him. He was like an uncle. In the dim light of the parking lot, he cornered her against the driver’s side door. She remembers the smell of his sandalwood cologne and the greasy taste of the *ladoo* he had pressed into her hand earlier. She froze. She did not scream. She did not fight. When it was over, he straightened his kurta, patted her shoulder, and said, “Let’s not make this awkward for our families.”

Amara drove home in silence. She showered for an hour. She told no one.

The next morning, she went to the shop as usual. But the sanctuary was gone. The first time a male customer—a kind, elderly man buying turmeric—reached past her to grab a bag, she flinched so violently she knocked over a display of pickles. She apologized, laughing too loud, her heart hammering. She began to dread the shop. The bell above the door became a trigger. Every time it jingled, her stomach dropped. She started working only in the back room, sorting inventory, leaving Raj to handle the counter. She told him she had a backache.

At home, intimacy vanished. When Raj touched her shoulder at night, she would go rigid, her breath shallow. She started sleeping in their daughter’s room, claiming the child had nightmares. She avoids the temple now. She avoids the community WhatsApp group. She has not told her mother, who lives in Mumbai, because her mother would “die of shame.” The secret is a hot stone in her chest.

Her PCL-5 score of 72 reflects the severity of her symptoms. She has recurrent, intrusive images of the parking lot—the way the gravel crunched under his shoes. She has nightmares where she is drowning in a sea of rice, unable to scream. She avoids the smell of sandalwood, which means she can no longer enter the incense aisle of her own shop. She is hypervigilant: she checks the back seat of her car every morning, even though she parks in her own driveway. She has started locking the bathroom door when she showers, something she never did before.

She feels a profound, corrosive guilt. She replays the moment: *Why didn’t I knee him? Why did I say “thank you” when he let me go?* She believes she is damaged goods, that she invited it by wearing a bindi that night, by smiling too much. She has not cried in months. She describes herself as “a hollow pot.”

Her marriage is fraying. Raj is confused and hurt. He thinks she is depressed, possibly menopausal. He has suggested she see a doctor for her “mood.” She cannot tell him the truth. She fears he will see her as sullied, or worse, that he will confront the man and bring violence upon their family. So she smiles, she nods, and she disappears further into the back room of her own life.

She came to therapy only because her daughter’s school counselor noticed the child was drawing pictures of people with no mouths. Amara does not think she deserves help. She is here because she is terrified of passing this silence on to her daughter. She sits in the chair, clutching her purse, waiting to see if this room, too, will become unsafe.
